newsitem.title: GERMANY: Daimler-Benz overhaul plan almost finished.
newsitem.headline: Daimler-Benz overhaul plan almost finished.

text.p: German industrial giant Daimler-Benz AG has told managers that a plan to shake up its structure is almost complete despite signs that powerful Mercedes-Benz head Helmut Werner remains opposed.

Chairman Juergen Schrempp and finance chief Manfred Gentz wrote in a letter to managers dated November 26 and seen by Reuters on Sunday that the management board had settled on a model to submit for supervisory board approval on January 23.

But the news weekly Der Spiegel reported that Werner, head of Daimler's cash cow Mercedes-Benz, had not agreed to the plan and was continuing to lobby openly against limiting the luxury car maker's independence.
Schrempp wants to dissolve the Mercedes management and put Mercedes directly under the control of the Daimler board.
In their letter, Schrempp and Gentz said management and planning at Daimler were too complicated and time-consuming. Profitability had risen, but was still unsatisfactory.
"Committees talk to committees, headquarters report to other headquarters," the letter said. "Central managements must also make their contribution."

Der Spiegel quoted from a rival letter, which it said Werner had sent to Daimler's top management. His letter apparently told them he could not approve the plan because it had "a number of systemic weaknesses which have not been eliminated".

Werner, who threatened to resign in October when news of the restructuring first emerged, added that he believed these weaknesses could be dealt with when details of the plan were worked out, Spiegel said.
"The image of the company has been visibly damaged" by the public spat, Werner added.
A Daimler spokesman could not confirm the details of the Werner letter.
Daimler posted a record 5.7 billion mark loss in 1995 and omitted a dividend for the first time in over four decades.
In the first half of 1996, it returned to the black with a profit of 728 million marks, and was expected to pay a dividend this year.
The board has been debating for months how to make the group's management more efficient. In October six board members were said to have approved the basic plan, while only Werner opposed it.
The plan is in line with Schrempp's stated intention when he took office in May 1995 to reduce the group's 35 business divisions to 11. -- Bonn newsroom, 49 228 26097150
